newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bajaj hit by slower sales, taxes.
newsitem.headline: India's Bajaj hit by slower sales, taxes.

text.p: Indian scooter and motorcycle maker Bajaj Auto on Wednesday announced sluggish growth for the financial year ended March 31 due to an industrial slowdown that hit vehicle sales during the period.
Bajaj Auto -- among the world's largest makers of two- and three-wheelers -- announced a modest five percent rise in net profit to 4.40 billion rupees, from 4.18 billion in 1995/96.
The firm's net profit had surged nearly 40 percent in 1995/96 from the previous year.
"The second half according to me was a disaster," chairman Rahul Bajaj told analysts and journalists at a post-results meeting. "It was not a satisfactory situation."
He said weak sales growth was due to an industrial slowdown that has depressed demand for consumer durables since the middle of calendar 1996.
Vehicle sales rose to 1.42 million units from 1.31 million the previous year. The firm had targeted 1996/97 sales of 1.55 million units.
"I don't have a crystal ball," Bajaj said, when he was asked to forecast sales for the current financial year.
Bajaj said lower demand had forced his firm to slash output to an average 4,600 units a day in the second half of 1996/97, from 5,100 units during the first six months of the year.
The results were a touch below expectations for automobile analysts who had already lowered their net profit forecasts to around 4.5 billion rupees.
They said sharply higher taxation at 2.36 billion rupees, against 1.77 billion in 1995/96, dragged the firm's net below forecasts.
"The biggest single problem was the provision for tax," Bajaj said.

Bajaj said leasing proposals worth 1.8 billion rupees had yielded a tax break for the company in the previous year. Due to regulatory changes in 1996/97, the firm did not participate in such transactions, he said.

Increasing competition saw the firm's market share in scooters drop to 69.1 percent, from 70.5 percent. The firm's share in mopeds fell to 9.4 percent from 11.1 percent due to the delayed launch of its 60cc "Cygnet" model.
Its share in the motorcycle market climbed to 31.1 percent during 1996/97, from 29.5 percent in the previous year.
Bajaj shares ended 65.50 rupees, or 7.7 percent, higher at 915.25 on the Bombay bourse despite the sluggish results.
Traders said the stock surged after the firm announced its board would meet to announce a bonus issue of equity shares.
But the firm's chairman said after trading hours he was not in favour of issuing a bonus in the proportion of one share for every share held.
"My strong recommendation to the board would be not to issue one-for-one bonus shares," Bajaj said at the meeting.
He said exports fell to 1.58 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 1.89 billion a year ago, and targeted exports of 2.0 billion rupees in the current year.
